title: Plan-and-Execute Agents
summary: A plan-and-execute agent splits the work in two: a planner reads the goal once and emits an explicit, ordered list of steps, then an executor carries out each step (often with tools) without re-deciding the whole strategy every turn. When a step fails or reality diverges from the plan, a replanner revises the remaining steps. Separating planning from execution buys you a cheaper, more auditable, more parallelizable loop than pure ReAct — at the cost of a plan that can go stale.
nestedConcepts: the step list as a contract

subtopics.title: Two roles: planner and executor
subtopics.explanation: A planner is one LLM call whose only job is to turn a goal into an ordered list of concrete steps. An executor then performs each step, usually with tools, without re-reasoning about the entire strategy on every turn. Splitting the roles is the core idea, because it lets each part be optimized — a strong model for planning, a cheap or specialized one for execution.

subtopics.title: The step list is a contract
subtopics.explanation: The planner's output is a structured, ordered plan — ideally typed (each step has an action and arguments) so the executor can consume it deterministically. Because the plan is explicit data, you can log it, show it to a human for approval, or even edit it before running. Making the plan a first-class artifact is what turns an opaque agent into an auditable one.

subtopics.title: Execute steps in order, collecting results
subtopics.explanation: The executor walks the plan step by step, feeding each step's result forward so later steps can use earlier outputs. Independent steps can even run in parallel, which a per-turn ReAct loop cannot do. Executing a pre-made plan is cheaper per step because the executor is not re-deriving the whole strategy on every model call.
subtopics.example:
results = {}
for i, step in enumerate(plan.steps):
    # earlier results are available to later steps
    out = executor(step, prior=results)
    results[i] = out
final = synthesize(results)
# no full re-planning per step -> fewer, cheaper decisions

subtopics.title: Replan when a step fails
subtopics.explanation: Reality diverges from plans: a search returns nothing, a tool errors, an assumption was wrong. A replanner takes the goal, the completed steps, and the failure, and produces a revised set of remaining steps. Replanning is what keeps plan-and-execute from being brittle — it recovers the adaptivity that a static plan gives up.

subtopics.title: Plan-and-execute vs ReAct
subtopics.explanation: ReAct interleaves thinking and acting every turn, so it adapts constantly but pays for a full reasoning call at each step and can wander. Plan-and-execute reasons once up front, then executes cheaply, replanning only on failure — fewer expensive calls and a clearer audit trail, but a plan that can go stale between replans. Knowing this tradeoff is how you pick the right loop for a task's cost and predictability needs.
subtopics.example:
# ReAct: reason + act EVERY turn (adaptive, more calls)
# thought -> action -> observation -> thought -> action -> ...

# Plan-and-execute: reason ONCE, then act cheaply
# plan -> [step, step, step] -> (replan only if a step fails)
# same goal, different cost/adaptivity balance

foundations.overview: Plan-and-execute is an orchestration pattern that separates deciding what to do from doing it. A planner LLM reads the goal a single time and emits an explicit, ordered list of steps; an executor then carries out those steps — typically calling tools — without re-deriving the whole strategy on every turn. Because the plan is concrete data, you can log it, gate it behind human approval, or run independent steps in parallel. When execution diverges from the plan (a tool fails, a search comes back empty, an assumption breaks), a replanner takes the goal, the work completed so far, and the failure, and rewrites the remaining steps. The pattern trades some of ReAct's turn-by-turn adaptivity for fewer expensive reasoning calls, better predictability, and an auditable trail. The durable insight is that planning and execution are different jobs with different cost profiles, and splitting them lets you optimize and control each independently.
foundations.formalDefinition: A plan-and-execute agent is a two-phase orchestration in which a planner maps a goal to an ordered sequence of steps P = [s1, s2, ..., sn], an executor performs each step (possibly with tools) passing prior results forward, and a replanner regenerates the remaining steps whenever a step fails or the observed state contradicts the plan, repeating until the goal is met or a budget is exhausted.
foundations.whyItMatters: Pure ReAct pays for a full reasoning call on every step and can drift on long tasks. Separating a single planning phase from cheap execution reduces the number of expensive model calls, makes the agent's intended strategy inspectable before anything runs, and enables parallelism — all of which matter for cost, safety, and reliability at scale.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a project manager and a crew. The manager (planner) writes the work order once — an ordered checklist. The crew (executor) works the checklist without re-planning the project at every task. If a task hits a wall, the crew reports back and the manager revises the rest of the checklist (replanning). ReAct, by contrast, is one very smart worker who stops to rethink the entire project after every single task.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Multi-step research agents that plan a query/read/synthesize sequence; data pipelines where an agent plans extract/transform/validate/load steps; travel or booking assistants that lay out a plan and adjust when an option is unavailable; and coding agents that draft a plan of file edits and tests before executing them.
commonUseCases: Long multi-step tasks where per-turn re-reasoning is wasteful
Workflows needing human approval of the plan before execution
Tasks with independent sub-steps that can run in parallel
Situations demanding an auditable record of intended strategy

commonMisconceptions.myth: A plan-and-execute agent never adapts once it starts.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It adapts through replanning: when a step fails or the world contradicts the plan, a replanner rewrites the remaining steps. It just doesn't re-reason on every single turn like ReAct.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Plan-and-execute is always cheaper than ReAct.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's cheaper when the plan holds, because execution avoids full reasoning per step. But a task that replans constantly can cost as much as or more than ReAct — the savings depend on plan stability.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The plan must be followed exactly as written.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The plan is a starting contract, not a straitjacket. Good systems treat it as revisable state and expect the replanner to edit remaining steps as execution reveals new information.

codeLab.title: Build a plan-execute-replan loop with a step budget
codeLab.instructions: Implement run(goal, planner, executor, replanner, max_iters=10). It must: (1) call planner(goal) once to get a list of step dicts; (2) execute steps in order via executor(step, results) where results is a list of prior outputs, appending each return value to results; (3) if executor raises StepFailed, call replanner(goal, results, error_message) to get a NEW list of remaining steps and continue from those (do not lose results already collected); (4) count every executor attempt against max_iters and raise RuntimeError('budget exceeded') if the budget runs out; (5) return results when the step list is empty. Complete run so the harness passes.

checkpoints.prompt: What is the defining structural difference between plan-and-execute and ReAct?
options: Plan-and-execute reasons once up front then executes cheaply, replanning only on failure; ReAct reasons every turn
checkpoints.explanation: ReAct interleaves reasoning and acting on every turn. Plan-and-execute does the strategic reasoning once, executes the resulting steps cheaply, and only invokes a replanner when a step fails or the plan goes stale.

checkpoints.prompt: This replan branch loses progress. What's wrong?
options: Clearing results on replan throws away completed steps, so the replanner sees no history and later steps redo work
replanner needs the step, not the error
checkpoints.explanation: Replanning should revise the remaining steps while preserving what's already done. Resetting results to [] erases progress and starves the replanner of the context it needs to adapt intelligently.

checkpoints.prompt: How many times is the planner called for a plan that runs cleanly?
checkpoints.explanation: The planner is invoked a single time before execution. In plan-and-execute, additional planner-level calls happen only via the replanner on failure — a clean run plans once.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the replan call so it revises only the remaining steps with full context.
checkpoints.codeBefore:
except StepFailed as e:
    plan = replanner(goal,
checkpoints.explanation: The replanner needs the completed results (what's already been done) plus the goal and the error to decide the revised remaining steps. Passing results is what lets it adapt without redoing work.

theory.question: Explain the plan-and-execute pattern and its main tradeoffs versus ReAct.
theory.directAnswer: Plan-and-execute separates a single planning phase (turn the goal into an ordered step list) from an execution phase (perform each step with tools, passing results forward), with a replanner revising the remaining steps when one fails. Versus ReAct, it makes fewer expensive reasoning calls, produces an inspectable/approvable plan, and can parallelize independent steps; the tradeoff is that a plan can go stale between replans and, if replanning is frequent, the cost advantage erodes.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A two-phase orchestration pattern that decouples deciding what to do from doing it, with replanning as the recovery mechanism.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because re-reasoning about the entire strategy on every turn (ReAct) is expensive and can drift on long tasks, while a single up-front plan is cheaper to execute and auditable.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A planner emits an ordered list of typed steps; an executor runs them in order feeding outputs forward; on failure a replanner takes the goal, completed work, and error to regenerate the remaining steps, looping until done or budget-exhausted.

theory.whyImportant: It's a core lever for controlling cost, adaptivity, and auditability in agent design, and interviewers use it to test whether you can reason about when constant re-reasoning is wasteful.
theory.realWorldExample: A research agent plans 'search, read top 3, synthesize' once, executes cheaply, and only replans when a source returns nothing — far fewer full-reasoning calls than a ReAct loop that rethinks after every observation.

followUps.question: When does ReAct beat plan-and-execute?
followUps.answer: On short, highly unpredictable tasks where nearly every step changes the strategy, so up-front planning provides little value and would just be replanned constantly.

followUps.question: How do you keep replanning from looping forever?
followUps.answer: Bound total steps/attempts with a budget, and treat exhaustion as a routed failure — the same stopping-condition discipline every agent loop needs.

theory.question: Why make the plan an explicit typed artifact, and what does that enable?
theory.directAnswer: Because a concrete, ordered, typed plan turns an opaque agent into an inspectable one. You can log it for debugging, show it to a human for approval before execution, edit it, validate each step's arguments against a schema, and run independent steps in parallel — none of which is possible when the strategy lives implicitly inside a per-turn reasoning loop.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The design choice to represent the planner's output as structured data (e.g. a pydantic Plan of typed Steps) rather than free text or hidden state.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Agents that act in the real world need auditability, human oversight, and deterministic execution, all of which require the plan to be first-class data.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The planner emits a schema-conforming plan; the executor validates and consumes it; humans or guardrails can approve or edit it; and the runtime can schedule independent steps concurrently because dependencies are explicit.

theory.whyImportant: Explicit plans are what make plan-and-execute safer and more debuggable than an opaque loop, which matters for any agent touching production systems.
theory.realWorldExample: A finance agent's refund plan is shown to an operator who approves it before any money moves; because the plan is typed data, the approval UI and the audit log are trivial to build.

followUps.question: How does an explicit plan enable parallelism?
followUps.answer: When steps declare their dependencies, the runtime can run independent steps concurrently instead of strictly sequentially, cutting wall-clock time.

followUps.question: What's the risk of over-structuring the plan?
followUps.answer: Too rigid a schema can stop the planner from expressing needed steps; you balance structure (for validation/audit) against enough flexibility to handle the task.

scenario.question: A ReAct research agent is accurate but slow and expensive because it makes a full reasoning call after every tool result. How would you redesign it, and what would you watch?
scenario.directAnswer: Convert it to plan-and-execute: have a strong model produce one ordered plan (search, read, synthesize), execute steps with a cheaper model or direct tool calls, run independent reads in parallel, and replan only when a step fails. Watch the replan rate — if plans go stale so often that you replan on most tasks, the cost savings vanish and you may need a hybrid or to keep ReAct for the unpredictable parts.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A cost/latency optimization that trades per-turn reasoning for a single planning phase plus cheap execution.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: ReAct's full reasoning call per step dominates cost and latency on long tasks, and much of that reasoning is redundant when the overall strategy is stable.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Introduce a planner and typed plan, execute steps (parallelizing independent ones) with minimal reasoning, add a replanner for failures, and instrument the replan rate and per-task call count to confirm the savings are real.

scenario.whyImportant: It demonstrates matching the orchestration pattern to a task's stability and cost profile rather than defaulting to one loop everywhere.
scenario.realWorldExample: After switching, the team saw model calls per task drop by more than half and latency fall thanks to parallel reads; because sources were mostly reliable, the replan rate stayed low and the savings held.

followUps.question: What if the replan rate turned out high?
followUps.answer: Either the tasks are too unpredictable for up-front planning (favor ReAct) or the planner's steps are too fine-grained; coarsen steps or use a hybrid that plans milestones and ReActs within them.

followUps.question: How do you parallelize safely?
followUps.answer: Only run steps with no data dependency concurrently, cap concurrency to respect rate limits, and merge results deterministically before the synthesis step.

coding.question: Implement a plan-and-execute driver that plans once, executes steps in order passing prior results forward, replans on a failed step, and enforces a step budget.
coding.thoughtProcess: I plan a single time, then loop while steps remain. Each executor call gets the accumulated results so later steps can use earlier outputs. A StepFailed exception triggers a replan that returns the revised remaining steps while I keep the results already gathered. Every executor attempt counts against a budget so a repeatedly-failing plan can't loop forever.
lineByLine: planner(goal) is called exactly once, producing the initial ordered step list.
results accumulates each step's output so later steps can build on earlier ones.
attempts counts executor calls; checking it against max_iters bounds the whole run.
We pop the next step and execute it, passing the accumulated results forward.
On StepFailed we replan: replanner returns the revised remaining steps while results is preserved.
When the plan list empties, the goal is complete and we return the collected results.
The __main__ demo shows a failing middle step triggering one replan and the run still completing.
coding.timeComplexity: O(m) executor/replanner calls where m <= max_iters; per-call cost is dominated by tool/model work.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(m) for the results list plus the current remaining plan.

followUps.question: How would you add parallel execution?
followUps.answer: Have the planner mark step dependencies; execute steps with no unmet dependency concurrently, cap concurrency, and merge outputs before dependent steps run.

followUps.question: How would you detect a stale plan without a hard failure?
followUps.answer: After each step, compare observed state to the plan's assumptions and trigger a replan if they diverge, not only on exceptions.

keyTakeaways: Plan-and-execute splits the loop into a planner (goal -> ordered steps) and an executor (perform each step with tools), reasoning once instead of every turn.
Make the plan an explicit typed artifact so it can be logged, approved by a human, validated, and parallelized.
Replanning — regenerating the remaining steps from the goal, completed work, and the failure — is what restores adaptivity the static plan gives up.
Versus ReAct: fewer expensive reasoning calls, better auditability and parallelism, at the cost of a plan that can go stale between replans.
Bound total steps/attempts with a budget and preserve completed results across replans so a repeatedly-failing plan can't loop forever.
